name: Earthquake
tipsIntro: Five items above (sturdy rope, water-resistant matches, fire extinguisher, baby wrap, and head/neck protection) come from sources that name an earthquake-specific kit. The behaviours below are what the sources stress once the shaking starts or stops:

tips.text: Taiwan's whole bag series is built around this scenario: keep the bag by the door so it can be grabbed immediately if a building is damaged and evacuation is required.
Store roughly 3 days of food per person at home (in addition to your bag), and secure heavy furniture to the wall so it can't topple.
Put on sturdy shoes before moving around afterward — broken glass on the floor is a common injury source.
If trapped under debris, use a whistle, a torchlight, or tap on a pipe or wall to attract rescuers' attention — shouting tires you out and risks inhaling dust.
If pinned down, move periodically to prevent blood clots, and keep your spirits up while waiting for rescue.
Keep calm and douse any open flames immediately; take cover under sturdy furniture, away from glass.
After the shaking stops, check for a gas leak before using any flame — open windows, shut off the main valve, and report it rather than lighting anything.
Know how to give first aid and how to use a fire extinguisher — practise both before you need them.
A stroller is hard to manoeuvre over debris; a baby wrap or carrier is easier to evacuate with. If sheltering in place, use a cushion, folded clothing or a thick book to protect your head and neck.

name: Flood
tagline: Rising water from storms, rivers, or coastal surge
tipsIntro: The sourced documents mostly focus on evacuation behaviour for floods rather than flood-only gear — the one addition is South Korea's Safe Korea heavy-rain guide, which adds a portable burner (see the checklist above). Otherwise, the core kit doubles as your flood bag; below is what the sources emphasise doing with it.

tips.text: Move to higher ground. Stay put but grab your bag and be ready to evacuate the moment authorities advise it.
If it feels dangerous to remain home, call the emergency line and evacuate immediately, away from open areas, streams and storm drains.
Don't walk through moving water higher than ankle height; if you must, use a stick to check the ground ahead of you.
Flooding is more likely in low-lying or poorly-drained areas — check drains and clear blockages before the rainy season.
If your home is at risk, leave early and shelter elsewhere until the rain subsides.
In coastal or low-lying areas, a storm surge can flood the shoreline with little warning — move to high ground immediately and contact the police if you need help.
Stock at least 3 days of food and water per person and keep it together in one place; also fill your bathtub in advance as a backup water supply in case the mains are cut.
Fuel your car ahead of time or arrange transport with a neighbour, and clean drains and gutters and inspect nearby slopes/retaining walls before heavy rain arrives.

name: Typhoon
tagline: Tropical storms with high winds & flooding
tipsIntro: No items beyond the core kit were uniquely specified for typhoons — checking Taiwan's and South Korea's live sites confirmed this, though both add useful home-hardening steps alongside the bag. The sources put particular weight on a few items and behaviours as storms escalate:

tips.text: Keep a flashlight and first aid kit within reach — they're specifically called out for the power outages and storm-related injuries typhoons cause.
Set your freezer to its lowest setting ahead of time to slow food spoilage if the power goes out.
Tune in to the radio for updates throughout the storm — don't step outside during a lull, as winds can pick up again.

Hong Kong grades storms on an escalating signal system (No. 1 through No. 10); as the signal rises, finish your preparations, stay indoors and lock windows and doors, and keep monitoring radio or TV broadcasts.
A storm surge riding on a high tide can flood coastal areas — residents in low-lying coastal areas should move to high ground and contact police if assistance is needed.
At home, lay in sandbags and waterproof flood gates, clear your gutters, and reinforce or bring in windows, signage and hanging planters before the storm arrives.
Apply safety film or tape to windows, place sandbags or water barriers at basement entrances, and move parked vehicles and loose outdoor objects to safety.
